name: Publication Bias
description: The tendency for studies with positive, statistically significant, or novel results to be published, cited, and built upon far more readily than studies with null or inconclusive results -- systematically inflating the apparent size and reliability of an effect in the published literature relative to its true magnitude.
design_relevance_note: This corpus's own most directly self-critical entry: applied specifically to the nudge/choice-architecture literature that underlies much of this graph's Choice Architecture & Value Framing cluster, bias-corrected reanalysis of the nudge-effectiveness literature found the combined effect for entire categories of nudges (information, assistance) may be close to zero once publication bias is accounted for -- a genuine caution against assuming every cited 'nudge works' finding survives that correction.
myth_risk_note: Any single cited 'nudge increases X by Y%' figure drawn from the pre-2021 choice-architecture literature carries a real, quantified risk of being inflated by publication bias -- the corrected combined effect for entire nudge categories (information, assistance) may be close to zero, while defaults/structure-type interventions appear more robust. Worth checking which category a specific cited nudge falls into before treating its effect size as settled.
prevalence_note: A foundational meta-science concept underlying how much weight any single cited effect size should carry, though (like the closely related Replication Crisis) discussed far more in academic/methodology circles than everyday design-practice vocabulary.

findings.description: A systematic review of nudging techniques used in HCI/technology-mediated design research identifies 6 core cognitive-bias mechanisms and 23 distinct nudge design techniques, but finds the field lacks consensus on how to reliably design for and evaluate nudge effectiveness — many published applications don't clearly report which underlying mechanism they actually target.
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the 2019 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (ACM)

findings.description: Of 156 reviewed nudge studies (422 interventions), 74% were single-setting effectiveness checks rather than studies of moderators/mechanisms; only 24% explored why or when nudges work; only 7% used power analysis; only 2% used reporting-quality guidelines; 0% were preregistered.
findings.source_title: A Systematic Scoping Review of the Choice Architecture Movement: Toward Understanding When and Why Nudges Work

findings.description: Once Mertens et al.'s own dataset is re-analyzed with bias-correction (robust Bayesian meta-analysis), the combined effect drops to approximately d = 0.04 (BF01 = 0.95) — evidence against an effect in the 'information' and 'assistance' intervention categories; evidence for 'structure' interventions remains undecided rather than disproven.
findings.source_title: No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)

findings.description: The meta-analysis itself detects moderate publication bias toward positive results in the underlying nudge literature, via Egger regression.
findings.source_title: The effectiveness of nudging: A meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions across behavioral domains
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)

applications.title: A meta-meta-analysis finding only 'weak evidence' for publication bias across psychology and medicine
applications.description: Robbie van Aert and co-authors' 'meta-meta-analysis' (a systematic analysis of many meta-analyses) tested for publication bias across a sample of psychology and medicine studies, using only meta-analyses with homogeneous effect sizes (since most publication-bias-detection methods don't perform well under heterogeneity). The results diverged from prior research showing 'rather strong indications for publication bias,' instead finding only weak evidence for its prevalence, with mild bias affecting psychology and medicine similarly.
applications.ethical_note: An important complicating nuance for this entry, not a contradiction to smooth over: this corpus's other publication-bias evidence (Mertens, Szaszi, Maier et al.) documents a specific, severe case within the nudge/choice-architecture literature specifically, while this broader cross-field meta-meta-analysis suggests publication bias's overall prevalence across psychology and medicine may be milder than commonly assumed -- both can be true at once (a severe problem in one specific literature, a milder average across the field as a whole), and neither should be read as generalizing to the other.

applications.title: Studies finding a bilingual brain benefit were twice as likely to get published
applications.description: A 2015 study by de Bruin, Treccani, and Della Sala (published in Psychological Science, covered by Scientific American and the Association for Psychological Science) examined conference presentations on whether speaking multiple languages confers cognitive benefits. They found that studies presented at conferences which reported a cognitive advantage for bilingualism were almost twice as likely to eventually appear in a peer-reviewed journal as studies that found no such advantage -- a direct, quantified demonstration of publication bias in a specific, real, still-active research literature (bilingualism and cognition), distinct from this corpus's existing nudge-literature publication-bias evidence.
applications.ethical_note: A methodological self-critique within academic psycholinguistics, included here as a concrete, domain-specific instance of publication bias distinct from this corpus's existing nudge-literature evidence for the same bias.
